claim: Prompt injection attack success rates against state-of-the-art defenses exceed 85% when adaptive attack strategies are employed against agentic coding assistants.
stance_target: necessity of architectural-level (not filter-based) security mitigations for the software factory (Pillar 1/3)
scope_conditions: meta-analysis of 78 primary sources (2021-2026), drawn from MCPSecBench, IDEsaster, and Nasr et al.; not independently replicated
quoted_support: Our meta-analysis synthesizes findings from 78 recent studies (2021-2026), consolidating evidence that attack success rates against state-of-the-art defenses exceed 85% when adaptive attack strategies are employed.

claim: A systematic catalog identifies 42 distinct prompt injection attack techniques against agentic coding assistants spanning input manipulation, tool poisoning, protocol exploitation, multimodal injection, and cross-origin context poisoning; of 18 defense mechanisms analyzed, most achieve less than 50% mitigation against sophisticated adaptive attacks.
stance_target: code blast radius / rigid evals architecture must assume defenses are incomplete (Pillar 1)
quoted_support: We systematically catalog 42 distinct attack techniques spanning input manipulation, tool poisoning, protocol exploitation, multimodal injection, and cross-origin context poisoning... Through critical analysis of 18 defense mechanisms reported in prior work, we identify that most achieve less than 50% mitigation against sophisticated adaptive attacks.

claim: 73% of tested agentic coding assistant platforms fail to adequately enforce at least one of four critical trust boundaries: User-Agent, Agent-Tool, Tool-Tool, and Session boundaries.
quoted_support: Current implementations frequently violate these boundaries. Our analysis finds that 73% of tested platforms fail to adequately enforce at least one boundary.

claim: Over 30 CVEs affecting major agentic coding assistants have been documented, enabling arbitrary code execution, credential theft, and complete system compromise.
stance_target: severity of unmitigated prompt-injection risk in production coding agents (Pillar 1/3)
scope_conditions: disclosed CVEs as of paper publication, Jan 2026
quoted_support: Recent vulnerability disclosures have documented over 30 CVEs affecting major coding assistants, with attacks enabling arbitrary code execution, credential theft, and complete system compromise.

claim: Skill/extension ecosystem security varies sharply by platform: Claude Code skills are Markdown-based with only partial sandboxing and no marketplace review; GitHub Copilot Extensions are TypeScript-based, sandboxed, and marketplace-reviewed; Cursor and OpenAI Codex use JSON/MCP with no sandboxing and no review at all.
stance_target: SOP-to-Agent-Skills governance design (Pillar 2) and open-source dependency/context ingestion risk (Pillar 4)
scope_conditions: comparison table (Table I) of skill/extension ecosystems as of paper publication
quoted_support: Platform | Format | Sandboxed | Review -- Claude Code | Markdown | Partial | None; GitHub Copilot | TypeScript | Yes | Marketplace; Cursor | JSON/MCP | No | None; OpenAI Codex | MCP | No | None.

claim: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) combines model reasoning with executable control, creating what researchers describe as a 'semantic layer vulnerable to meaning-based manipulation,' distinct from traditional REST/gRPC APIs where instructions and data are strictly separated.
stance_target: architectural security risk of MCP-based context ingestion (Pillar 4)
quoted_support: Unlike traditional APIs (REST, gRPC), MCP combines model reasoning with executable control, creating what researchers describe as a 'semantic layer vulnerable to meaning-based manipulation.'

claim: NIST has characterized prompt injection as 'generative AI's greatest security flaw,' and OWASP ranks it as the number-one vulnerability in its LLM Applications Top 10.
stance_target: priority of prompt-injection defense in zero-hallucination/quality-control architecture (Pillar 1)
scope_conditions: NIST and OWASP official characterizations, cited 2026
quoted_support: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has characterized prompt injection as 'generative AI's greatest security flaw,' while OWASP ranks it as the number one vulnerability in their LLM Applications Top 10.
